title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV
2026-07-29 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) formerly known as Firepower Management Center contains a use of hard-coded password vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to log in to an affected device using a low-privileged account to access sensitive data within the impacted systems. Vendor: Cisco, Product: Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC). Federal patch due: 2026-08-01.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20316")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents

        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse dependency present (< 2.0.2, CVE-2026-54658) AIExploitation High
Inventories hosts/containers where the @hypequery/clickhouse npm package is installed (node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse) or flagged by TVM for CVE-2026-54658. This is the first-line exposure hunt for the SQL-injection-in-escapeValue advisory before any exploitation is attempted. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable package coordinate (@hypequery/clickhouse) and node_modules path plus the assigned CVE-2026-54658; a package-present hunt is the highest-confidence exposure signal for a dependency advisory with no IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/advisories/
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/CI build agents that legitimately install the package as part of the app
  • Hosts already upgraded to 2.0.2+ (file-presence check can't read the installed version)
  • npm/yarn offline mirror or cache directories holding the tarball
  • Monorepos with multiple hoisted copies of the package inflating FileCount
  • Container base-image scanning sandboxes that pull all dependency versions
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "2.0.2" and toint(split(SoftwareVersion, ".")[0]) < 2
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each host, confirm the installed version — read package.json/package-lock.json under @hypequery/clickhouse and check whether it is < 2.0.2; cross-reference the TVM CveId hit. Step 2 (contain): For confirmed <2.0.2 on internet-facing/user-facing services, prioritise `npm install @hypequery/clickhouse@2.0.2` (or later) and redeploy; there is no runtime workaround per the advisory. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC-2/UC-3 web and DB query-log detections for that host to determine whether the injection was already attempted before patching.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

@hypequery/clickhouse SQLi: backslash-quote escape bypass in web/API request parameters AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP/WAF request parameters that carry the CVE-2026-54658 exploitation primitive — a value with a trailing backslash immediately preceding a single quote (raw \' or URL-encoded %5C%27) — combined with SQL follow-on keywords. This is the on-the-wire signature of an attacker escaping the closing quote emitted by escapeValue(). Rationale: Encodes the article's precise exploitation mechanic — 'trailing backslash to escape the closing quote' — as a backslash-quote (\' / %5C%27) token gated by SQL keywords, so it fires on the injection attempt rather than a generic SQLi template. Requires the app to sit behind a WAF/reverse-proxy that logs request payloads; Defender has no web-log table (left empty). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei/Acunetix) running authorised SQLi test payloads
  • Legitimate query strings containing Windows paths ending in a backslash before a quoted value
  • Analytics dashboards passing ClickHouse system.* table names in URL filters
  • Encoded file paths in file-manager apps producing %5C sequences
  • Pen-test engagements from known internal source IPs
Suppression filter
| where DestinationHostName !has_any ("scanner", "appsec", "pentest") and SourceIP !in ("10.10.10.0")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the RequestURL/Payload and confirm the backslash precedes the string-terminating quote (not a legitimate escaped path); note SourceIP, destination host and whether the target app depends on @hypequery/clickhouse (UC-1). Step 2 (contain): Block the SourceIP at the WAF and, if the target is <2.0.2, take the endpoint out of rotation / apply the 2.0.2 upgrade. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the same SourceIP across other parameters/endpoints and pivot to UC-3/UC-4 on the backend DB host to confirm whether the injected SQL actually executed.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| extend Payload = strcat(tostring(RequestURL), " ", tostring(RequestContext), " ", tostring(Message))
| where Payload matches regex @"(?i)(\\'|%5c%27)"
| where Payload has_any ("UNION", "SELECT", "OR 1=1", "OR%201=1", " OR ", "--", "/*", "system.", "FROM system")
| where isempty(SourceUserName) or SourceUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Payload
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SQL injection backslash-quote escape in web request (CVE-2026-54658 primitive)
id: 7b2c8f14-3d6a-4e29-9f5b-8a1c0e7d6b52

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.t1190
logsource:

detection:
  escape:
    c-uri-query|contains:
      - "\\'"
      - '%5C%27'
      - '%5c%27'
  sqlkw:
    c-uri-query|contains:
      - 'UNION'
      - 'SELECT'
      - 'OR 1=1'
      - 'OR%201=1'
      - '--'
      - 'system.'
  condition: escape and sqlkw
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*%5C%27*" OR Web.url="*%5c%27*" OR Web.url="*\\'*") AND (Web.url="*UNION*" OR Web.url="*SELECT*" OR Web.url="*OR%201=1*" OR Web.url="*--*" OR Web.url="*system.*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*%5C%27*" OR Web.url="*%5c%27*" OR Web.url="*\\'*") AND (Web.url="*UNION*" OR Web.url="*SELECT*" OR Web.url="*OR%201=1*" OR Web.url="*--*" OR Web.url="*system.*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
ClickHouse query_log shows injected SQL from @hypequery escapeValue bypass AIExploitation Medium
Hunts ClickHouse server/query logs (shipped via Syslog) for statements containing the backslash-quote escape artifact together with injection follow-on SQL (UNION, OR 1=1, access to system.* tables). This is where CVE-2026-54658 exploitation becomes visible as actually-executed arbitrary SQL on the database tier. Rationale: Targets the backend evidence of 'arbitrary SQL execution' by matching the same backslash-quote artifact plus injection keywords in ClickHouse query logs; higher fidelity than the web-edge UC because it confirms the statement reached and parsed on the DB. Depends on ClickHouse logs being forwarded to Syslog/Datadog (noted); no Defender equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application queries that read from ClickHouse system.* tables (dashboards, monitoring)
  • Data-migration or admin scripts using UNION for legitimate merges
  • String literals in analytics data that naturally contain \' sequences
  • Query replay from load-testing tools
  • Backup/ETL jobs enumerating system.parts or system.tables
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full matching query and its originating user/client from query_log; determine whether the backslash-quote breaks out of a parameter string vs. appearing inside a legitimate literal. Step 2 (contain): If injection is confirmed, revoke the DB user/API credential the app uses, isolate the app host, and force the 2.0.2 upgrade. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all queries from the same client_id/initial_user around the event for data-exfiltration (SELECT from sensitive tables), and correlate back to the UC-2 web request that delivered the payload.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName has "clickhouse" or SyslogMessage has "clickhouse"
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(\\'|%5c%27)"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("UNION", "OR 1=1", " OR ", "system.", "FROM system", "--", "/*")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:clickhouse-server (*\\'* OR *%5c%27*) AND (*UNION* OR *"OR 1=1"* OR *system.* OR *"FROM system"*)
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=clickhouse OR sourcetype=clickhouse:query_log OR source="*clickhouse-server*")
| regex _raw="(?i)(\\'|%5c%27)"
| search ("UNION" OR "OR 1=1" OR " OR 1=1" OR "system." OR "FROM system" OR "--")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(host) as hosts by _raw
| sort - count
ClickHouse SQL syntax-error spike from @hypequery/clickhouse injection probing AIExploitation Low
Threshold hunt for a burst of ClickHouse SYNTAX_ERROR (Code: 62) / escapeValue-related exceptions on an application host, indicating an attacker iterating backslash-quote payloads against CVE-2026-54658 before a working injection lands. Failed injection attempts leave parser errors even when the successful one does not. Rationale: Names the article's escapeValue() function and the vulnerable package, plus ClickHouse's SYNTAX_ERROR code (62) that malformed injection payloads trigger; an error-rate spike is a cheap early-warning for injection fuzzing that the pattern-match UCs may miss when payloads are encoded. Telemetry depends on app/DB error logs reaching Syslog/Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Buggy application release emitting genuine malformed queries after a deploy
  • Developer/analyst ad-hoc query session with typos against the same ClickHouse
  • Schema-migration window where queries reference not-yet-created columns
  • BI tool generating invalid SQL for unsupported functions
  • Load/chaos testing that intentionally sends malformed statements
Suppression filter
| where Sample !has_any ("migration", "ALTER TABLE", "CREATE TABLE")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the sample error messages and the client/user generating them — a single external client driving the spike with backslash-quote payloads is malicious; a recent app deploy is likely benign. Step 2 (contain): If external and injection-shaped, block the source at the WAF, revoke the app's DB credential, and schedule the 2.0.2 upgrade. Step 3 (hunt): Look for one successful (non-error) query from the same client immediately after the error burst (the payload that worked) and pivot to UC-3 to assess data access.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where (SyslogMessage has "Code: 62" and SyslogMessage has "Syntax error") or SyslogMessage has "escapeValue" or SyslogMessage has "@hypequery/clickhouse"
| summarize ErrCount = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where ErrCount > 20   // 20 = burst threshold: normal apps emit near-zero ClickHouse syntax errors per 5m
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:clickhouse-server ((*"Code: 62"* AND *"Syntax error"*) OR *escapeValue* OR *@hypequery/clickhouse*)
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=clickhouse OR sourcetype=clickhouse:query_log OR source="*clickhouse-server*")
| search ("Code: 62" "Syntax error") OR "escapeValue" OR "@hypequery/clickhouse"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as errCount values(host) as hosts by _time
| where errCount > 20
| sort - _time
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54658")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54658")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-54658")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-54658")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Hunts the CVE-2026-64863 exploit signature where an attacker probes the --no-delete restriction (DELETE returns 403) and then destroys the same resource via the WebDAV MOVE verb (201 Created / 204 No Content). The 403-then-2xx pairing on an identical URL within a short window is the bypass fingerprint, not generic WebDAV usage. Rationale: Uses the article's exact control-vs-bypass pairing: DELETE=403 (blocked by --no-delete) then MOVE=201/204 (RemoveAll/rename succeeds). Correlating both on the same URL from the same source removes benign WebDAV MOVE traffic, which never co-occurs with a just-refused DELETE on the identical path. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A WebDAV sync client (Finder/Explorer) that retries a delete as a rename after a transient 403 for reasons unrelated to policy
  • Automated backup tooling that first attempts DELETE, is denied, and falls back to MOVE-to-archive on the same object
  • Load/security scanners (e.g. Nessus WebDAV checks) exercising both verbs against the same test path
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites and duplicates request lines, double-logging one client action as two verbs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target server is goshs (<= v2.1.3) — check the response Server header 'goshs/...' and whether it was launched with '-w --no-delete'; pull the full request sequence for the src IP against the affected URL. 2) Contain: block the src IP at the WAF/proxy and stop/upgrade the goshs instance to v2.1.4 (or drop WebDAV write verbs MOVE/COPY at the proxy) so the --no-delete boundary is actually enforced. 3) Hunt: enumerate every MOVE 201/204 from that src across all served paths to scope which artefacts were renamed away or overwritten, and check file integrity of the served directory against a known-good manifest.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod in ("DELETE","MOVE")
| extend DeleteBlocked = iff(csMethod == "DELETE" and scStatus == 403, 1, 0)
| extend MoveSuccess = iff(csMethod == "MOVE" and scStatus in (201, 204), 1, 0)
| where DeleteBlocked == 1 or MoveSuccess == 1
| summarize DeleteBlocked = sum(DeleteBlocked), MoveSuccess = sum(MoveSuccess), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(scStatus) by cIP, csUriStem, Computer, sSiteName
| where DeleteBlocked > 0 and MoveSuccess > 0
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="DELETE" AND Web.status=403) OR (Web.http_method="MOVE" AND Web.status IN (201,204)) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.dest_port, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval delete_blocked=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status=="403",1,0)
| eval move_success=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status=="201" OR status=="204"),1,0)
| stats sum(delete_blocked) as delete_blocked, sum(move_success) as move_success, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(status) as statuses by src, dest, dest_port, url
| where delete_blocked>0 AND move_success>0
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="DELETE" AND Web.status=403) OR (Web.http_method="MOVE" AND Web.status IN (201,204)) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.dest_port, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval delete_blocked=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status=="403",1,0)
| eval move_success=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status=="201" OR status=="204"),1,0)
| stats sum(delete_blocked) as delete_blocked, sum(move_success) as move_success, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(status) as statuses by src, dest, dest_port, url
| where delete_blocked>0 AND move_success>0
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
WebDAV MOVE/COPY write-verb succeeds against goshs artifact server (Overwrite:T destination clobber) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful WebDAV MOVE/COPY verbs (201/204) against an exposed goshs file server, the mechanism CVE-2026-64863 abuses to rename-away or, with the 'Overwrite: T' header, RemoveAll and overwrite existing files under --no-delete. MOVE/COPY are rare in normal artifact-download traffic, so a success is a high-signal exploitation candidate. Rationale: Keys on the article's exploitation primitive — the WebDAV MOVE/COPY verbs returning 201/204 — plus the 'Overwrite: T' header called out as the RemoveAll trigger (grep RequestContext/Message where the WAF logs headers). MOVE/COPY are near-absent in legitimate file-download workloads, so a success against a goshs host is worth a hunt even without correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-50138/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV clients (Finder, Windows Explorer, Cyberduck) renaming files on a genuinely writable goshs share (no --no-delete set)
  • CI/CD or backup jobs that use MOVE to atomically publish artifacts into the served directory
  • SharePoint/Nextcloud or other WebDAV appliances behind the same WAF that legitimately use MOVE/COPY
  • Web content-management operations issuing COPY for versioning
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a goshs instance and whether it runs with --no-delete/--read-only; inspect the request for a 'Destination:' and 'Overwrite: T' header (header-logging WAFs) that indicates intent to clobber an existing file. 2) Contain: strip MOVE/COPY at the proxy for that vhost and upgrade goshs to v2.1.4; restrict the WebDAV port to trusted source ranges. 3) Hunt: pivot on the src IP to list all MOVE/COPY targets and any preceding blocked DELETE (see companion rule) to determine which served files were destroyed or overwritten.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestMethod in ("MOVE", "COPY")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs process deletes or renames served files while launched with --no-delete (impact confirmation) AIActions on Objectives High
Confirms real data loss from CVE-2026-64863 on the host: a goshs process removing or renaming files (os.Rename / RemoveAll) even though it was started with --no-delete. Under that flag goshs should never delete anything, so any goshs-initiated file delete/rename event is a direct policy violation and proof the WebDAV MOVE bypass fired. Rationale: Combines the article's process (goshs) with its stated invariant (--no-delete means no deletion) — so a goshs-initiated FileDeleted/FileRenamed with '--no-delete' on the command line is a definitional bypass with essentially no benign explanation. This is the on-host impact confirmation for the HTTP-layer rules. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://github.com/goshs-labs/goshs/releases
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • goshs writing/cleaning up transient files for the ?bulk zip-download feature (temporary archive creation, not served-file deletion)
  • An operator manually deleting files in the served directory with another tool (would not show goshs as the initiating process)
  • goshs launched without --no-delete performing intended deletes (excluded by the --no-delete command-line filter)
  • Log-rotation or the goshs binary being self-updated/replaced on disk (rename of the binary rather than served content)
Suppression filter
// Defender: exclude self-update/binary replacement and keep only served-content paths
| where not (FileName endswith "goshs" or FileName endswith "goshs.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm --no-delete/--webdav were set, and capture FolderPath/PreviousFolderPath to identify exactly which served file was renamed or removed. 2) Contain: stop the goshs service and upgrade to v2.1.4 (or remove WebDAV); restore the affected file(s) from backup, as MOVE/RemoveAll destroys the original content. 3) Hunt: correlate the file event timestamp back to the WebDAV access log for the matching MOVE 201/204 and its source IP to attribute the actor, and review whether other files in the same directory disappeared in the same window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "goshs"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted", "FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, PreviousFolderPath, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted", "FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs SFTP launch: empty-credential basic-auth (-b 'user:' / ':pass') with -sftp and no -fkf AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact vulnerable configuration for CVE-2026-62325 / CVE-2026-40884: a goshs process started with -sftp and a -b basic-auth string that has an empty username or empty password, and without -fkf (public-key). This combination disables the SFTP PasswordHandler (gliderlabs/ssh sets NoClientAuth=true), exposing unauthenticated file read/write/delete/rename. Article-specific because it keys on the literal goshs binary and its -b/-sftp/-fkf flag semantics, not a generic SSH check. Rationale: Uses the article's literal vulnerable invocation `goshs -b 'admin:' -sftp` and the flag logic (`-b` empty-side + `-sftp` + absence of `-fkf`) that produces NoClientAuth=true. The empty-credential regex catches both the CVE-2026-62325 empty-password variant and the CVE-2026-40884 empty-username variant. Cross-checked against the SentinelOne CVE-2026-40884 entry and the GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
ATT&CKT1190 T1021.004 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pentester/red-team intentionally running goshs as a throwaway file server on an engagement host
  • CTF or lab boxes where goshs is deliberately started with weak auth for training
  • Automation/scripts that pass -b with a trailing colon by mistake but on an internal-only isolated host
  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("pentest", "redteam", "ctf", "lab") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("pentest", "redteam"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the exact `-b` value and whether `-fkf` is absent; identify the listening port and whether the host is internet-facing (check DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing / firewall NAT). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the goshs process and block the SFTP listener port at the host firewall; if internet-facing, treat as actively exploitable and isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2/UC3 — enumerate inbound SFTP connections this goshs PID accepted and every file it read/wrote/deleted; determine data exposure and whether any remote client IP is external.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
// empty-password ( user: ) or empty-username ( :pass ) in the -b basic-auth string
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+['""]?([^\s'"":]+:(?:['""]|\s|$)|:[^\s'""]+)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific: keys on the goshs process as the network-listening initiator rather than a generic SSH port. Rationale: Ties the network-listener behaviour to the specific goshs binary named throughout the article (impact: 'Unauthenticated SFTP file access'), so it flags exposure and live client connections rather than any SSH traffic. Anomalous Host header on Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints (CVE-2026-54588) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-54588 exploitation: requests to Poweradmin's /oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, or /logout endpoints carrying an HTTP Host header value that has never been seen for that site in the 30-day baseline. Poweradmin embeds HTTP_HOST verbatim into the redirect_uri/ACS URL sent to the IdP, so an attacker-controlled Host value is the exploitation primitive. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoints (/oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, LogoutController) and the root-cause primitive (untrusted HTTP_HOST embedded in callback URLs). Baseline anti-join surfaces the attacker's poisoned Host (e.g. attacker.com) without hardcoding the victim's legit hostname. Cross-checked GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx and SentinelOne/NVD (CWE-20/601, CVSS 9.6). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54588
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new vhost/hostname added to the Poweradmin front-end (rename, new DNS name, migration)
  • Uptime/health-check probes (Pingdom, StatusCake) that send synthetic Host headers
  • Load-balancer or Kubernetes ingress health probes hitting endpoints with pod-IP Host values
  • Vulnerability scanners run by the org's own security team (Nessus/Burp) sending crafted Host headers
  • CDN/WAF origin pulls that rewrite the Host to an internal origin name
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1") and CsHost !endswith ".internal" and CsHost !endswith ".svc.cluster.local" and not (CsUserAgent has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to the anomalous CsHost on the auth endpoints; confirm the Host value is not an owned domain and check whether the request produced a 301/302 to an IdP authorize URL (redirect_uri would contain the attacker host). 2) Contain: set interface.base_url in Poweradmin config/settings.php (activates the safe branch immediately) and upgrade to 4.2.4/4.3.3; fix the reverse proxy so it does not pass proxy_set_header Host $http_host. 3) Hunt: check the IdP for AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch events and any successful admin sign-ins in the hour that followed; audit PowerDNS zones (MX, SPF/DKIM, CAA, delegation) for unauthorized changes.

    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(LookbackDays) .. ago(RecentHours))
    | where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
    | summarize by CsHost;

Host header fuzzing burst against Poweradmin auth endpoints from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects unauthenticated reconnaissance/injection probing for CVE-2026-54588: a single source IP hitting Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints with 2+ distinct HTTP Host header values inside a 10-minute window. This is the shape of an attacker enumerating which flow reflects HTTP_HOST into the outbound redirect_uri. Rationale: Self-contained fan-out on the article's specific auth endpoints; multiple distinct Host headers from one IP is the unambiguous signature of host-header injection probing described in the advisory (unauthenticated, no credentials required). No allowlist/placeholder needed. Thresholds (2 hosts, 3 requests) are conservative and self-evident from the attack shape. Spike of AADSTS50011 redirect_uri mismatch at IdP (poisoned Poweradmin callback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the IdP-side footprint of CVE-2026-54588 when the OIDC/SAML IdP is Entra ID: a burst of AADSTS50011 (redirect_uri / reply-URL mismatch) failures on a single application within an hour. Entra rejects the attacker-poisoned redirect_uri (attacker.com/oidc/callback) because it is not a registered reply URL, so a cluster of 50011 on the Poweradmin app is high-fidelity evidence of active redirect_uri poisoning. Rationale: Directly maps the article's exploitation mechanic (poisoned redirect_uri sent to the IdP) to the IdP error it produces. Corroborated by Microsoft Learn / SSOJet: AADSTS50011 'spiking on URIs you never deployed' is the documented signature of an attacker probing crafted redirect_uri values — exactly this CVE. 5/hr threshold separates probing from a single stray config typo. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app-registration reply-URL misconfiguration after a Poweradmin upgrade or hostname change
  • A single trailing-slash / http-vs-https typo in the app's configured base_url producing repeated 50011 for legit users
  • Developer/staging instance of Poweradmin pointed at the production app registration
  • Reply-URL propagation lag (~60s) right after an admin edits the app registration
  • Load-balanced deployment where one node has a stale/incorrect base_url
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIPs has_any ("10.","192.168.") and Users == 1)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the failing redirect_uri/reply-URL values in the sign-in detail — legit misconfig repeats one owned URL, an attack shows external/attacker hostnames or many distinct URIs. 2) Contain: if attacker hosts are present, treat affected users as at-risk (revoke sessions/refresh tokens for any who authenticated), lock the app to strict reply-URL matching, and force Poweradmin's interface.base_url + patch. 3) Hunt: pivot to successful sign-ins for the same users from new IPs in the following hour (see companion UC), and audit PowerDNS zones for MX/SPF/DKIM/CAA tampering.

| summarize AttemptCount=count(), Users=dcount(AccountUpn), UserList=make_set(AccountUpn,20), SrcIPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by Application, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 5   // 5+ reply-URL mismatches/hr on one app = probing, not a one-off config typo
| order by AttemptCount desc

Victim account takeover: new-IP sign-in within 1h of redirect_uri mismatch (CVE-2026-54588) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates the two halves of a successful CVE-2026-54588 account takeover on Entra: a successful sign-in for a user from an IP absent from their 90-day baseline, occurring within one hour of an AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch event for that same user. Catches the case where the attacker captured the victim's authorization code via a poisoned redirect_uri and then used it/logged in. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #1 and ties the article's stated outcome ('IdP redirects the victim's authorization code to an attacker' → full account takeover, no credentials) to observable telemetry: a fresh-IP success closely following a 50011 for the same user. Baseline anti-join + 1h temporal window is high-fidelity and article-specific to the redirect-poisoning flow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User travels / switches to a new mobile-carrier or home IP the same hour a legit 50011 config error fired
  • VPN or corporate-proxy egress-IP rotation introducing a 'new' IP for an existing user
  • New device enrollment where the user re-auths from an unfamiliar network after an app-registration reply-URL fix
  • Roaming user behind CGNAT whose apparent IP changes between the failure and the success
  • Admin testing the app registration (deliberately triggering 50011) then logging in from a lab network
Suppression filter
| where DelayMin <= 60 and NewIP !startswith "10." and NewIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the success IP's geo/ASN vs the user's baseline and whether the 50011 FailIP differs; check what the session did next (consent grants, PowerDNS zone edits, mail-flow rules). 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, force password reset + re-MFA, and block the new IP; if the user is a Poweradmin admin, freeze PowerDNS zone changes. 3) Hunt: review PowerDNS for MX hijack, SPF/DKIM additions, CAA removals and subdomain delegation; sweep other users for the same 50011→new-IP pattern and confirm the app is patched (4.2.4/4.3.3) with interface.base_url set.
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where ErrorCode == 50011
    | project FailTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, FailIP = IPAddress, Application;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, NewIP = IPAddress, Country, Application, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where ResultType == "50011"
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, FailIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, NewIP = IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc

Tengu Botnet Reboots Compromised Linux Devices When Defenders Kill Its Process

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Mirai-derived botnet called Tengu can use a compromised Linux device's hardware watchdog to trigger a reboot when defenders kill its main process. If that happens, Tengu's other persistence mechanisms get another chance to relaunch it. Nozomi Networks Labs observed the dropper reaching its honeypots through Telnet credential brute force. Tengu supports 25 distributed denial-of-service (

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities · [LLM] Tengu guardian process masquerading as kernel thread [kworker/0:0] · [LLM] Tengu immutable-binary persistence via chattr +i on Linux/IoT
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts high-volume inbound Telnet (TCP/23) connection attempts from a single external source against Linux/IoT hosts, the entry vector Nozomi observed for the Tengu dropper on its honeypots. Article-specific because Tengu spreads exclusively via Telnet default/weak-credential brute force rather than an exploit. Rationale: Uses the article's stated entry vector (Telnet TCP/23 credential brute force on internet-exposed IoT/Linux) as a volumetric single-source pivot; port 23 to public-facing embedded hosts is inherently high-signal since legitimate Telnet exposure is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1110 T1078.001 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal network/security scanner (Shodan-style, Nessus, Nmap) sweeping TCP/23 across the estate
  • A misconfigured legacy management tool that legitimately polls Telnet on embedded gear
  • ISP/upstream background internet scanning noise hitting an exposed device
  • Load-balancer or NAT health checks probing port 23
  • Penetration-test engagement against IoT segment
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target hosts are IoT/embedded and that TCP/23 is genuinely internet-reachable; check whether any attempt succeeded (post-auth session, new process). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, disable/firewall Telnet on the exposed devices, and rotate any default credentials. 3) Hunt: on any device that accepted a session, pivot to Tengu post-compromise indicators — outbound TCP/9931 to 64.89.163.8, a process masquerading as [kworker/0:0], chattr +i on new binaries, and modified /sbin/reboot|shutdown utilities.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where LocalPort == 23 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceId), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP
| where Attempts > 20   // empirical Telnet brute-force volume threshold from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 23
| summarize Attempts = count(), Denied = countif(DeviceAction in~ ("deny","drop","blocked","reset")), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where Attempts > 20   // brute-force volume threshold on Telnet/23 from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any egress from an internal host to the hardcoded Tengu C2 IP 64.89.163.8 over TCP/9931 (plaintext registration/heartbeat) or TCP/8080 (IPFS gateway payload retrieval). Article-specific because both the IP and the two ports are named in the analyzed sample's configuration. Rationale: The C2 IP 64.89.163.8 and both ports (9931 for plaintext registration/heartbeat, 8080 for the IPFS gateway) are explicit strings from the analyzed sample; a hardcoded single-IP + non-standard-port pair is near-zero-FP. URLhaus independently logged 17 malicious Mirai-related URLs at the same IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html • https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/host/64.89.163.8/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001 T1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate IPFS node/user on the estate happening to reach port 8080 on that host (unlikely — IP is a known-bad C2)
  • Threat-intel or sandbox detonation VM deliberately beaconing to the IOC during analysis
  • Security researcher/blue-team validating the IOC from a lab host
  • Stale NAT/proxy log attributing the connection to the wrong internal source
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source device and the initiating process (Defender InitiatingProcessFileName / Falcon ContextImageFileName); confirm the host is IoT/Linux. 2) Contain: block 64.89.163.8 at the perimeter, isolate the device from the network, and preserve volatile state before power actions (Tengu corrupts reboot/shutdown binaries). 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts beaconing to the same IP/ports, and on the infected host review systemd units, /etc/init.d, /etc/rc.local, shell rc files, cron, and /dev/watchdog before reimaging.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where RemotePort in (9931, 8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where DestinationPort in (9931, 8080)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHost = SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc
