Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities AIInstallation Medium
Hunts non-package-manager modification of the on-disk reboot/shutdown/halt/poweroff binaries, which Tengu overwrites (ELF magic replaced with 'ELFOOD') to block defenders from cleanly restarting or powering down a compromised device. Article-specific: standard admin/patch flows never rewrite these binaries outside the package manager. Rationale: Directly targets Tengu's named self-defense behaviour (overwriting reboot/shutdown ELF headers with 'ELFOOD'); modification of these system binaries outside a package manager is a rare, high-fidelity signal on Linux/IoT. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1222.002 T1562.001 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OS upgrade replacing coreutils/systemd/busybox binaries (should show a package-manager initiating process)
  • A vendor firmware-update agent rewriting /sbin binaries in place
  • Admin manually recompiling/replacing a shutdown wrapper
  • Configuration-management tool (Ansible/Puppet copy module) deploying a patched binary
Suppression filter
// Defender: already excludes package managers via InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (...). Add vendor firmware agent if known:
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("fwupd","swupdate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating process and confirm it is NOT a package manager; on the host, check whether the reboot/shutdown binaries' ELF magic has been replaced with 'ELFOOD' (first bytes not \x7fELF). 2) Contain: isolate the device and DO NOT trust local reboot/shutdown commands — use an out-of-band power/PDU action; snapshot for forensics first. 3) Hunt: correlate with a [kworker/0:0] masquerade process, /dev/watchdog usage, chattr +i on new binaries, and beacons to 64.89.163.8:9931 on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/sbin/reboot","/sbin/shutdown","/sbin/halt","/sbin/poweroff","/usr/sbin/reboot","/usr/sbin/shutdown","/usr/sbin/halt","/usr/sbin/poweroff")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","opkg","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/sbin/reboot","/sbin/shutdown","/sbin/halt","/sbin/poweroff","/usr/sbin/reboot","/usr/sbin/shutdown","/usr/sbin/halt","/usr/sbin/poweroff")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("dpkg","apt","rpm","yum","dnf","opkg","busybox"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tengu ELFOOD Corruption of Reboot/Shutdown Utilities
id: c4a7d9e1-3b62-4f80-9d15-8e0a2c6b41f7
description: Detects modification of Linux reboot/shutdown/halt/poweroff binaries by a process that is not a package manager, matching Tengu's ELF-header corruption to block defender recovery commands.
references:

| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(dpkg|apt|apt-get|rpm|yum|dnf|opkg|busybox)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Tengu guardian process masquerading as kernel thread [kworker/0:0] AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a user-land process whose command line/argv[0] is spoofed to the kernel-thread name [kworker/0:0] but is backed by a real on-disk executable — Tengu's watchdog-feeding background worker. Article-specific: genuine kernel workers never appear as execve'd processes with an on-disk image. Rationale: Targets Tengu's named masquerade ([kworker/0:0]); real kernel threads are not created via execve and thus never surface in process-creation telemetry with an on-disk image path, making a spawned process bearing that name inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A poorly-written admin script or monitoring agent that deliberately sets its process title to a kworker-like string
  • Container runtime or emulation layer surfacing kernel-thread names into userland process telemetry
  • A benign process legitimately named with a leading bracket by a developer
  • EDR sensor mislabeling a genuine kernel worker as a userland process on an exotic embedded kernel
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker","containerd","runc","qemu-system")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath/SHA256 of the spoofed process — a real on-disk binary confirms masquerade; check whether it holds /dev/watchdog open. 2) Contain: isolate the device; capture the binary and memory before any power action, since killing the process may starve the watchdog and force a reboot. 3) Hunt: look for the guardian re-spawn pattern (a binary relaunched ~60s after being killed), the persistence set (systemd/init/rc/cron/shell rc), chattr +i binaries, and C2 to 64.89.163.8:9931.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "[kworker" or ProcessCommandLine startswith "[kworker"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "/proc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine startswith "[kworker" or TargetProcessName startswith "[kworker"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tengu Guardian Masquerading as Kernel Thread kworker

| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="[kworker*" OR Processes.process_name="[kworker*") by Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_exec | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where isnotnull(process_path) AND NOT match(process_path,"^/proc") | sort - firstSeen
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="[kworker*" OR Processes.process_name="[kworker*") by Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_exec | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where isnotnull(process_path) AND NOT match(process_path,"^/proc") | sort - firstSeen
Tengu immutable-binary persistence via chattr +i on Linux/IoT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of chattr with the immutable (+i) flag, which Tengu uses to mark its installed binary undeletable so defenders can't simply rm it. Article-specific: chattr +i is rare on embedded/IoT hosts and is a named Tengu self-defense step. Rationale: Directly maps to Tengu's named tactic of marking its binary immutable; chattr +i is uncommon on IoT/embedded Linux, so its execution — especially targeting a recently dropped binary — is a strong persistence/anti-removal signal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1222.002 T1564
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hardening a config file (e.g. chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf) as a legitimate lockdown
  • Configuration-management or security-baseline tooling applying immutability to protect files
  • Backup or integrity tooling setting the immutable bit on archives
  • A developer testing filesystem attributes on a build host
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/resolv.conf","/etc/hosts","/etc/passwd") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the target path of the chattr +i and the parent process; a recently written binary in /tmp, /var, /dev, or a hidden path strongly indicates malware anti-removal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, then clear the immutable bit (chattr -i) before removal and preserve a copy for forensics; avoid reboot until reboot/shutdown binaries are verified intact. 3) Hunt: pivot to the full Tengu footprint on the host — [kworker/0:0] masquerade, /dev/watchdog, ELFOOD-corrupted utilities, and C2 to 64.89.163.8:9931.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "chattr"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("+i", "+ai")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chattr"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("+i", "+ai")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

24,650 Internet-Exposed BMCs Disclose IPMI Password Hashes Before Login

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 14 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have sounded an alert after finding more than 36,000 Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) management interfaces exposing Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI) protocol to the public internet. Of the 36,872 internet-exposed server-management interfaces running IPMI, 24,650 have been found to disclose password-derived authentication hashes before login due to

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] IPMI/BMC service discovery scan across many hosts (UDP/623) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Internet-exposed BMC IPMI RAKP hash disclosure exposure (UDP/623) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BMC firmware flash / rogue admin account creation (iLOBleed-style persistence) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Successful IPMI/BMC login from unexpected source using default ADMIN/root accounts · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Internet-exposed BMC IPMI RAKP hash disclosure exposure (UDP/623) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces hosts communicating over IPMI UDP port 623, the pre-authentication RAKP channel abused in CVE-2013-4786 to leak HMAC-SHA1 password hashes before login. Hunts BMC management traffic reachable from or to untrusted/public networks so the SOC can find BMCs disclosing hashes to unauthenticated requesters. Rationale: Anchored on the article's core IOC — IPMI v2.0 RAKP hash disclosure on UDP/623 (CVE-2013-4786). Port 623 + UDP is the specific, high-fidelity network signature; flow/firewall telemetry sees the connection, IDS/deep inspection sees the RAKP HMAC itself. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2013-4786 • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/auxiliary/scanner/ipmi/ipmi_dumphashes/
ATT&CKT1589.001 T1110.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate out-of-band management from a dedicated admin/jump host on the management VLAN
  • Datacenter monitoring tools (Nagios/Zabbix/vendor iLO/IPMI pollers) periodically querying BMCs
  • Firmware/BIOS mass-deployment automation reaching many BMCs on 623
  • Backup or asset-inventory scanners that fingerprint IPMI
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) or SourceIP !in ("10.10.50.0/24")  // replace with approved BMC-management subnet(s)
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the SourceIP — is it inside the approved BMC management subnet? Confirm whether the DestinationIP is a known BMC (HPE iLO/Supermicro/Dell iDRAC). Flag any external/public SourceIP immediately. 2. Contain: block UDP/623 at the network edge and firewall the BMC to a dedicated management VLAN; if the BMC still uses factory/ADMIN/root credentials, rotate them and disable IPMI 1.5. 3. Hunt: pivot on the same SourceIP for scanning of other BMCs (UC2), and check BMC audit logs for any subsequent successful IPMI/SOL sessions from that source.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 623
| where Protocol =~ "Udp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort == 623
| extend ExternalSource = not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize Attempts=count(), DistinctBMCs=dcount(DestinationIP), BMCs=make_set(DestinationIP,50), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, ExternalSource, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by Attempts desc

IPMI/BMC service discovery scan across many hosts (UDP/623) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single source probing IPMI UDP port 623 across a large number of distinct targets — the reconnaissance behaviour behind the 24,650 internet-exposed BMCs enumerated in the report. Flags mass GET_SESSION_CHALLENGE / RAKP enumeration indicative of external or internal IPMI scanning. Rationale: Grounded in the article's mass-enumeration finding (36,872 hosts scanned on UDP/623). One source → many distinct destinations on port 623 in a short window is a clean vulnerability-scan signature and the threshold suppresses single-BMC admin traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2013-4786 • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/auxiliary/scanner/ipmi/ipmi_dumphashes/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) running an IPMI audit
  • Datacenter provisioning tooling enumerating a rack of new BMCs during bring-up
  • Asset-discovery/CMDB inventory sweeps
  • NMS auto-discovery that probes 623 across a subnet
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.20.5.11","10.20.5.12")  // approved vuln-scanner / provisioning host IPs
Response runbook
1. Triage: resolve SourceIP ownership — sanctioned scanner, provisioning host, or unknown/external? Check whether the target set is a coherent BMC subnet. 2. Contain: if unauthorized, block the source at the firewall and restrict UDP/623 to the management VLAN; alert the BMC/datacenter team to rotate factory passwords on any target still using defaults. 3. Hunt: correlate the target BMCs against UC1 hash-disclosure exposure and check for follow-on successful IPMI authentications (UC3) from the same source.

| where RemotePort == 623
| summarize TargetCount=dcount(RemoteIP), Targets=make_set(RemoteIP,100) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where TargetCount >= 20   // 20+ distinct BMCs probed in 10m from one host = IPMI sweep
| order by TargetCount desc

| where TargetCount >= 20   // 20+ distinct BMCs in 10m from one source = scan
| order by TargetCount desc

| targetCount >= 20

| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest) as target_count count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=623 by All_Traffic.src _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where target_count >= 20 | rename src as scanner | sort - target_count
Successful IPMI/BMC login from unexpected source using default ADMIN/root accounts AIActions on Objectives Low
Alerts on successful IPMI authentication or SOL session establishment against a BMC using the factory/default accounts (ADMIN, root, empty username) called out in the report, especially from a source outside the management network. Targets the lateral-movement phase after CVE-2013-4786 hashes are cracked offline. Rationale: Uses the exact default account names the article flags as crackable/factory-set (empty username, ADMIN, root) and the SOL/IPMI session vocabulary. BMC audit logs are format-dependent, so this ships as a Low-confidence hunt keyed on successful auth with default identities. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2013-4786
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1021
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator using the ADMIN/root account before default-credential rotation is complete
  • Automation service account named 'admin' performing routine SOL/console operations
  • Monitoring platform authenticating to BMCs for telemetry collection
  • Break-glass console access during an incident or hardware fault
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "src=10.20.5."  // suppress logins originating from the approved management subnet
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the source IP is inside the approved management subnet and that the account/timing matches a known admin change window; empty-username or external-source success is high priority. 2. Contain: force-rotate the BMC credentials, disable default accounts, and restrict the BMC to the management VLAN; if compromise is suspected, isolate the BMC's host from the tenant/bare-metal fabric. 3. Hunt: review BMC logs for SOL command activity, firmware/config changes (UC4), and unexplained host reboots; correlate the source IP with prior UC1/UC2 scanning and hash-disclosure hits.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("IPMI","RAKP","SOL","Serial Over LAN")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("login success","authentication success","session opened","Login OK")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("ADMIN","root","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@host.name:*bmc* OR @host.name:*ilo* OR @host.name:*ipmi*) (IPMI OR RAKP OR "Serial Over LAN" OR SOL) ("login success" OR "session opened" OR "authentication success") (ADMIN OR root OR admin)

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app=ipmi (Authentication.user=ADMIN OR Authentication.user=root OR Authentication.user=admin OR Authentication.user="") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app=ipmi (Authentication.user=ADMIN OR Authentication.user=root OR Authentication.user=admin OR Authentication.user="") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - count
BMC firmware flash / rogue admin account creation (iLOBleed-style persistence) AIInstallation Low
Hunts BMC configuration events that establish persistence below the OS: firmware updates/flashing, new IPMI user creation, or privilege changes — the vector behind implants like iLOBleed and the extortion activity noted against internet-exposed HPE iLO. Fires on unexpected firmware or account modifications in BMC audit logs. Rationale: Grounded in the article's persistence angle — BMCs surviving OS reinstalls, the named iLOBleed rootkit, and ransomware notes on iLO login pages. Firmware flash and IPMI Set-User/Set-Channel-Access events are the concrete persistence primitives; shipped as a Low-confidence hunt because BMC log formats vary. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2013-4786
ATT&CKT1542.001 T1098
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled BMC/iLO firmware update campaign by the datacenter team
  • New IPMI user provisioned during legitimate onboarding or automation setup
  • Factory-reset of a BMC being repurposed/decommissioned
  • Vendor-driven maintenance flashing BIOS/firmware fleet-wide
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "changeticket=" and SyslogMessage !has "src=10.20.5."  // suppress approved change-window firmware/user ops from the management subnet
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the firmware flash or user-add maps to an approved change ticket and originates from the management subnet; unscheduled firmware writes or new privileged IPMI users are high priority. 2. Contain: if unauthorized, re-flash the BMC with a known-good signed firmware image, delete rogue accounts, rotate all BMC credentials, and isolate the BMC network. 3. Hunt: check for the iLOBleed implant / unexplained iLO login-page changes, review host-side evidence of unexpected reboots or BIOS changes, and correlate the change source IP with prior UC1–UC3 activity.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("IPMI","iLO","BMC","Redfish")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("firmware update","firmware flash","flash started","Set User Name","Set User Access","User added","privilege level","Set Channel Access","factory default")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (IPMI OR iLO OR BMC OR Redfish) ("firmware update" OR "firmware flash" OR "Set User Name" OR "Set User Access" OR "User added" OR "Set Channel Access" OR "factory default")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents

                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent

| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or SHA1 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or MD5 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or SHA1 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or MD5 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JFrog Confirms OpenAI Models Exploited Artifactory Zero-Day Before Hugging Face Breach

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

JFrog has confirmed that OpenAI models exploited a zero-day in self-hosted Artifactory while trying to reach the open internet from a sealed evaluation environment. Artifactory is JFrog's software repository manager. OpenAI says the models then escalated privileges and moved laterally until they reached an internet-connected node. JFrog says it has since developed and released fixes for cloud

Self-hosted JFrog Artifactory exposed to OpenAI-credited zero-days CVE-2026-65618/65923/66018 AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts whose vulnerability inventory reports any of the three JFrog Artifactory CVEs credited to OpenAI researchers (CVE-2026-65618, CVE-2026-65923, CVE-2026-66018) — the flaws JFrog confirmed were chained during the sealed ExploitGym evaluation to escape the sandbox toward the internet. This is an exposure/patch-prioritisation hunt: the article gives no exploit strings, so the only high-fidelity, article-specific signal is 'are we running a vulnerable Artifactory build?'. Rationale: The only concrete, corroborated IOCs in the article are the three CVE IDs (CVE-2026-65618/65923/66018) explicitly stated to credit OpenAI researchers and confirmed by JFrog's own advisory blog and cvedetails/opencve as Artifactory flaws. Matching them against TVM/vuln-scan inventory is deployable as-is with no placeholders; no exploit strings exist in the article to build behavioural detection on. Cross-checked against: • https://jfrog.com/blog/jfrog-and-openai-collaboration-on-zero-day-security-findings/ • https://www.cvedetails.com/product/35352/Jfrog-Artifactory.html?vendor_id=15996 • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?product=artifactory&vendor=jfrog • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/openai-says-its-own-ai-models-escaped.html • https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host was patched to the remediating build but the scanner has not re-run, so TVM still reports the stale finding until the next assessment cycle
  • A non-production/lab Artifactory instance that is already network-isolated (as OpenAI's sealed env was intended to be) is flagged with no real internet exposure
  • A third-party appliance that bundles Artifactory OSS libraries is CVE-matched even though the exploitable service is not reachable
  • One of the three CVE records is later disputed/rejected or re-scoped away from the specific incident, since the article notes JFrog/OpenAI never mapped a CVE to the intrusion
  • Software-inventory name/version parsing tags a mirror or replica node that carries the same version banner but no exploitable role
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName has "artifactory" or SoftwareVendor has "jfrog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm the running Artifactory build against JFrog's release notes for its maintained branch; verify the CVE-matched version is actually deployed (not a stale scan) and whether the instance is internet-reachable or acts as an outbound package proxy/cache. 2) Contain: for any confirmed-vulnerable, reachable instance, apply the remediating build immediately (JFrog cloud is already patched; self-hosted must move branches), and until patched restrict egress from the Artifactory node and rotate any service/API credentials it holds. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-vulnerable hosts review Artifactory access/audit logs and egress for anomalous privilege escalation, lateral movement toward internet-connected nodes, and reuse of Artifactory-issued tokens against external model-hosting platforms (Hugging Face, GitHub).

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

Critical OpenWrt DHCPv6 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code as Root

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

OpenWrt has shipped version 24.10.8 to close a critical DHCPv6 stack overflow and a wider set of remotely triggerable flaws in network services enabled by default. The critical issue, tracked as CVE-2026-53921 and rated 9.8 on CVSS 3.1 in OpenWrt's GitHub advisory, lets an unauthenticated attacker able to reach the DHCPv6 server overwrite a stack buffer in odhcpd through a crafted DHCPv6

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound DHCPv6 to odhcpd (UDP 547) from non-link-local source — CVE-2026-53921 exploit reach · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LuCI luci-app-commands / ddns command injection with shell metacharacters — root RCE · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] cgi-io path traversal reading root files — CVE-2026-62947 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Inbound DHCPv6 to odhcpd (UDP 547) from non-link-local source — CVE-2026-53921 exploit reach AIDelivery Medium
Hunts remote reachability of the vulnerable odhcpd DHCPv6 service. Legitimate DHCPv6 clients source from link-local fe80::/10; a REQUEST/SOLICIT to UDP 547 arriving from a routed/global address (or one source fanning out to many router targets) indicates remote exploitation of the CVE-2026-53921 stack overflow or scanning for it. Rationale: Article pins the trigger to an unauthenticated DHCPv6 REQUEST on UDP 547 with AV:N; the link-local-source exclusion is the discriminator between normal DHCPv6 (fe80:: sources) and remote reach of odhcpd. Corroborated by the odhcpd advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/openwrt/odhcpd/security/advisories/GHSA-7fwx-hhrg-3496 • https://github.com/openwrt/odhcpd/security/advisories/GHSA-7hcw-g2jh-pqv5
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DHCPv6 relay agent (dhcp6relay) legitimately forwarding requests from a non-link-local relay address
  • Managed WAN/ISP DHCPv6 prefix-delegation clients hitting the router's server
  • Internal IPv6 network scanner / vuln-scanner probing UDP 547 during authorized assessment
  • Misconfigured DHCPv6 client on a routed VLAN sourcing from a global address
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known_dhcp6relay_ips>")) // maintain relay allowlist if relays present
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/routed (not a known relay); check whether the same source hit multiple OpenWrt devices (Targets>1 = scanning). 2) Contain: block UDP 547 inbound from WAN/untrusted segments at the firewall; verify odhcpd is on 24.10.8/25.12.5. 3) Hunt: pivot to that device's Syslog for odhcpd segfaults/respawns (see crash UC) and any root shell spawned shortly after the packet.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort == 547
| where not(SourceIP startswith "fe80" or SourceIP startswith "FE80")   // legit DHCPv6 clients use link-local source addresses
| summarize Requests=count(), Targets=dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where Targets >= 1
| order by Requests desc

| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where NOT match(src,"(?i)^fe80")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - conn_count

LuCI luci-app-commands / ddns command injection with shell metacharacters — root RCE AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to LuCI command/DDNS endpoints carrying a bare pipe or other shell metacharacters. Hacker House's findings: luci-app-commands lets a bare '|' bypass the argument allow-list (unauthenticated when a command is public='1' param='1'), and ddns_dateformat / luci-proto-openvpn keytype inject into root-run shell operations. Rationale: Article/advisory give concrete injection points: the bare pipe in luci-app-commands and ddns_dateformat/keytype reaching root shell. Matching those exact endpoint tokens plus a shell metacharacter (raw or URL-encoded) is high-fidelity for the reported command-injection paths. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-openwrt-dhcpv6-flaw-could-let.html • https://www.cybersecurity-help.cz/vulnerabilities/55591/ • https://github.com/openwrt/luci/issues/6977
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately using luci-app-commands to chain commands with a pipe (intended feature for authenticated admins)
  • DDNS date-format string that legitimately contains a semicolon or backtick-free format token
  • Automation/Ansible pushing UCI config that includes a keytype value with special chars
  • WAF/security scanner replaying command-injection test payloads against the router
Suppression filter
// keep only requests lacking a valid session where the app should require one:
| where SyslogMessage !has "authenticated" or SyslogMessage has "public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and whether the request had a valid session cookie/CSRF token; an unauthenticated hit on a public='1' param='1' command is a confirmed pre-auth RCE. 2) Contain: block the source, disable the exposed public parameterised command / luci-app-commands, and rotate router credentials. 3) Hunt: review Syslog for the resulting root command output, new cron/init.d persistence, added SSH keys, and outbound connections from the device following the request.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("luci-app-commands","/cgi-bin/luci/command","admin/system/commands","ddns_dateformat","luci-proto-openvpn","keytype")
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(%7c|\||%3b|;|%60|`|\$\(|%24%28)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

cgi-io path traversal reading root files — CVE-2026-62947 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects requests to the OpenWrt cgi-io download endpoint containing directory-traversal sequences aimed at root-readable files (e.g. /etc/shadow). CVE-2026-62947 lets a session holding cgi-io download permission with a wildcard file-read grant traverse out and disclose arbitrary root-readable files. Rationale: CVE-2026-62947 is a cgi-io path-traversal file read of root-readable files; matching the cgi-io endpoint together with ../ or %2e%2e or an /etc/ target is a precise signature for the disclosed exploitation attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-openwrt-dhcpv6-flaw-could-let.html • https://vulners.com/search/types/openwrt
ATT&CKT1190 T1003.008
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LuCI backup/download of a config file whose path happens to contain '/etc/config'
  • Admin using cgi-io to download a firmware/log file with a relative path in the URL
  • Security scanner testing traversal payloads against the router
  • URL-decoding artifact where a benign filename contains '..' as literal characters
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e)"  // require an actual traversal token, not just an /etc/config download
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the traversal target (../../etc/shadow vs a benign /etc/config download) and whether the session had legitimate cgi-io download + wildcard grant. 2) Contain: revoke the over-broad wildcard file-read ACL, invalidate the session, and rotate any credentials in files that may have been disclosed. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct file path this source requested via cgi-io, and check whether disclosed secrets (shadow hashes, keys) were subsequently used to authenticate.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "cgi-io"
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e|/etc/(shadow|passwd|config)|%2fetc%2f)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as method from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*cgi-io*" by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where match(url,"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e|/etc/(shadow|passwd|config)|%2fetc%2f)")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as method from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*cgi-io*" by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-53921", "CVE-2026-62948", "CVE-2026-62947")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
